Introduction and meaning
Unlawful assembly (old 141/143): five or more persons with a common object of the listed kinds — overawing government, resisting law, committing mischief or criminal trespass, taking possession, compelling a person by force.
In student language: BNS s. 189 is the rule on “Unlawful assembly”. The section provides that (1) An assembly of five or more persons is designated an “unlawful assembly”, if the common object of the persons composing that assembly is—. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 189 exists so that “Unlawful assembly” has a closed legal test in Chapter XI — Of Offences Against the Public Tranquillity. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: Unlawful assembly, common object, rioting, affray, and promoting enmity.

The provision in detail
189. (1) An assembly of five or more persons is designated an “unlawful assembly”, if the common object of the persons composing that assembly is—

(a) to overawe by criminal force, or show of criminal force, the Central Government or any State Government or Parliament or the Legislature of any State, or any public servant in the exercise of the lawful power of such public servant; or

(b) to resist the execution of any law, or of any legal process; or

(c) to commit any mischief or criminal trespass, or other offence; or

(d) by means of criminal force, or show of criminal force, to any person, to take or obtain possession of any property, or to deprive any person of the enjoyment of a right of way, or of the use of water or other incorporeal right of which he is in possession or enjoyment, or to enforce any right or supposed right; or

(e) by means of criminal force, or show of criminal force, to compel any person to do what he is not legally bound to do, or to omit to do what he is legally entitled to do

Essential ingredients
1. (1) An assembly of five or more persons is designated an “unlawful assembly”, if the common object of the persons composing that assembly is—
2. (a) to overawe by criminal force, or show of criminal force, the Central Government or any State Government or Parliament or the Legislature of any State, or any public servant in the exercise of the lawful power of such public servant; or
3. (b) to resist the execution of any law, or of any legal process; or
4. (c) to commit any mischief or criminal trespass, or other offence; or
5. (d) by means of criminal force, or show of criminal force, to any person, to take or obtain possession of any property, or to deprive any person of the enjoyment of a right of way, or of the use of water or other incorporeal right of which he is in possession or enjoyment, or to enforce any right or supposed right; or
6. (e) by means of criminal force, or show of criminal force, to compel any person to do what he is not legally bound to do, or to omit to do what he is legally entitled to do

Explanations
Explanation.—An assembly which was not unlawful when it assembled, may subsequently become an unlawful assembly

(2) Whoever, being aware of facts which render any assembly an unlawful assembly, intentionally joins that assembly, or continues in it, is said to be a member of an unlawful assembly and such member shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine, or with both

(3) Whoever joins or continues in an unlawful assembly, knowing that such unlawful assembly has been commanded in the manner prescribed by law to disperse, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both

(4) Whoever, being armed with any deadly weapon, or with anything which, used as a weapon of offence, is likely to cause death, is a member of an unlawful assembly, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both

(5) Whoever knowingly joins or continues in any assembly of five or more persons likely to cause a disturbance of the public peace, after such assembly has been lawfully commanded to disperse, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine, or with both

Explanation.—If the assembly is an unlawful assembly within the meaning of sub-section (1), the offender shall be punishable under sub-section (3)

(6) Whoever hires or engages, or employs, or promotes, or connives at the hiring, engagement or employment of any person to join or become a member of any unlawful assembly, shall be punishable as a member of such unlawful assembly, and for any offence which may be committed by any such person as a member of such unlawful assembly in pursuance of such hiring, engagement or employment, in the same manner as if he had been a member of such unlawful assembly, or himself had committed such offence

(7) Whoever harbours, receives or assembles, in any house or premises in his occupation or charge, or under his control any persons knowing that such persons have been hired, engaged or employed, or are about to be hired, engaged or employed, to join or become members of an unlawful assembly, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine, or with both

(8) Whoever is engaged, or hired, or offers or attempts to be hired or engaged, to do or assist in doing any of the acts specified in sub-section (1), shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine, or with both

(9) Whoever, being so engaged or hired as referred to in sub-section (8), goes armed, or engages or offers to go armed, with any deadly weapon or with anything which used as a weapon of offence is likely to cause death, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both

hypotheticals.question: Whether BNS s. 189 (Unlawful assembly) applies, and how structured written arguments should be framed.
hypotheticals.analysis:
Step 1 — Identify the provision. The correct current-law cite is BNS s. 189 (Unlawful assembly), Chapter XI — Of Offences Against the Public Tranquillity.
Step 2 — State the legal test in your own words, then list the ingredients:
   (1) An assembly of five or more persons is designated an “unlawful assembly”, if the common object of the persons composing that assembly is—
   (2) (a) to overawe by criminal force, or show of criminal force, the Central Government or any State Government or Parliament or the Legislature of any State, or any public servant in the exercise of the lawful power of such public servant; or
   (3) (b) to resist the execution of any law, or of any legal process; or
   (4) (c) to commit any mischief or criminal trespass, or other offence; or
   (5) (d) by means of criminal force, or show of criminal force, to any person, to take or obtain possession of any property, or to deprive any person of the enjoyment of a right of way, or of the use of water or other incorporeal right of which he is in possession or enjoyment, or to enforce any right or supposed right; or
   (6) (e) by means of criminal force, or show of criminal force, to compel any person to do what he is not legally bound to do, or to omit to do what he is legally entitled to do
Step 3 — Read every Explanation. An explanation is part of the section. Omitting it leaves the analysis incomplete and vulnerable to rebuttal.
Step 4 — Map each fact to an ingredient. Write “this fact proves ingredient (a)” or “this fact is missing, so the section is not made out”.
Step 5 — Conclude. If every essential ingredient is proved and no exception covers the case, BNS s. 189 applies. If any essential ingredient fails, say so and stop. Do not invent a different section to save the answer.

enhancement.legalPrinciple: Criminalizes collective public disorder by defining any assembly of five or more persons with a shared unlawful common object as an unlawful assembly.

Core Legal Mandate: (1) An assembly of five or more persons is designated an “unlawful assembly”, if the common object of the persons composing that assembly is—
(a) to overawe by criminal force, or show of criminal forc...
Classification and Sentencing: Structured under Chapter XI penal tiers.
Evidentiary and Procedural Cognate: Governed by the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 and Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023.
essentialIngredients: (1) An assembly of five or more persons is designated an “unlawful assembly”, if the common object of the persons composing that assembly is—

(a) to overawe by criminal force, or show of criminal force, the Central Government or any State Government or Parliament or the Legislature of any State, or any public servant in the exercise of the lawful power of such public servant
(b) to resist the execution of any law, or of any legal process
(c) to commit any mischief or criminal trespass, or other offence
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 189 consolidates the definition (former IPC 141, 142) and general punishment (former IPC 143) of an unlawful assembly. An assembly becomes unlawful when it consists of five or more persons united by one of five enumerated common objects: overawing the Government or public servants, resisting the execution of any law or legal process, committing mischief or criminal trespass, forcibly depriving someone of property or right of way, or compelling any person to do an illegal act. An assembly that starts lawfully can become an unlawful assembly if a common unlawful object is adopted. Mere presence in an assembly without knowledge of or participation in the unlawful object does not create liability.
examples: Teaching example (Standard application): An individual intentionally commits acts satisfying the statutory formula of unlawful assembly under Section 189 without lawful authority. The individual is liable under BNS s. 189.

Teaching example (Absence of mens rea / Lawful exception): A person acts in good faith or without the requisite statutory mental element under circumstances recognized by law. The essential ingredients of Section 189 are not satisfied; no penal liability attaches.
distinctions: Unlawful Assembly (s. 189) vs Rioting (s. 191): An unlawful assembly is the static collective group with an unlawful object; Rioting occurs when force or violence is actually used by that assembly.

Unlawful Assembly vs Common Intention (s. 3(5)): Unlawful assembly requires at least 5 persons with an enumerated common object; Common intention applies to 2 or more persons sharing any prior criminal meeting of minds.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether the accused is liable under BNS s. 189 for conduct relating to unlawful assembly.
Rule: Under BNS s. 189, liability attaches upon proof of the statutory actus reus accompanied by the requisite mens rea without lawful justification.
Application: The evidence demonstrates that the accused performed the specified act with the required state of mind, satisfying all statutory ingredients of Section 189.
Conclusion: The accused is guilty of an offence under BNS s. 189 and subject to the prescribed punishment.
